clinicalPearls: Thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) is a pathologic lesion of endothelial injury in terminal arterioles and capillaries, with platelet and hyaline thrombi causing partial or complete occlusion; it is usually but not always accompanied by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) featuring thrombocytopenia and schistocytes.

Renal histology of TMA shows swollen endocapillary cells (endotheliosis), fibrin thrombi, platelet plugs, arterial intimal fibrosis, and a membranoproliferative glomerular pattern; fibrin thrombi may extend into the arteriolar pole producing glomerular collapse and at times cortical necrosis, and recovered kidneys may develop secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.

The classic TTP pentad (MAHA, thrombocytopenia, neurologic symptoms, fever, renal failure) is rare: fewer than 5% of immune-mediated TTP cases show the full pentad, so do not wait for all five to act.

TTP is defined as MAHA associated with ADAMTS13 activity below 5-10%; ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers accumulate, form clots, and shear erythrocytes, but loss of ADAMTS13 alone may need an additional trigger (infection, surgery, pancreatitis, pregnancy) to provoke clinical disease.

Atypical (complement-mediated) HUS reflects alternative complement pathway dysregulation; affected patients often have low C3 with normal C4, and factor H deficiency is the most common defect, with more than 70 factor H gene mutations described.

Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) HUS, classically D+ (diarrhea-associated) HUS, mostly affects children under 5 but can affect adults; bloody diarrhea precedes MAHA within one week in over 80% of cases, fever is typically absent, and neurologic involvement is common, especially in adults.

Scleroderma renal crisis presents with acute kidney injury, abrupt-onset hypertension, and a normal urine sediment (though none is strictly required); it occurs in about 12% of diffuse but only ~2% of limited systemic sclerosis, and its renal histology of 'onion-skinning' arcuate artery intimal/medial proliferation is indistinguishable from malignant hypertension.

Antiphospholipid syndrome produces a predisposition to arterial and venous thrombosis and recurrent fetal loss; 'triple positivity' (lupus anticoagulant, anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I, and anticardiolipin antibodies) carries the highest thrombosis risk, and APLS is the leading cause of stroke in patients under 45.

HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) is a microvascular pregnancy complication; the defining organ is the liver (subcapsular hematoma with potential rupture), renal failure occurs in about half of patients, and proteinuria is present in 86-100%.

Renal vein thrombosis can present with flank pain, tenderness, hematuria, rapid renal decline, and proteinuria, or be silent and discovered during a pulmonary embolism workup; the left renal vein is more commonly involved and two-thirds of cases are bilateral.

Sickle cell nephropathy arises from occlusion of the vasa recta in the renal medulla, where low oxygen tension and high osmolarity favor hemoglobin S polymerization and sickling; sequelae include hyposthenuria, hematuria, and papillary necrosis (which can also occur in sickle trait).

Drug-induced TMA occurs via two mechanisms: dose-dependent toxic/endothelial damage (chemotherapeutics such as proteasome inhibitors, mitomycin C, gemcitabine; immunosuppressives such as calcineurin inhibitors, interferon, sirolimus) or non-dose-dependent drug-induced autoantibodies (e.g., quinine, which can react even after a single re-exposure).
harrison.pathophysiology: Thrombotic renovascular disorders share endothelial injury of the renal microvasculature (terminal arterioles and capillaries) leading to platelet/hyaline thrombi and microangiopathic hemolysis. In TTP, deficient ADAMTS13 activity (below ~5-10%, from congenital mutation in cTTP/Upshaw-Schulman syndrome or acquired autoantibody in iTTP) allows ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers to accumulate, forming platelet-rich thrombi that shear red cells; an inflammatory trigger is often required to manifest disease. In atypical HUS, dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway (commonly factor H deficiency, or defects in factor I, factor B, CD46/membrane cofactor protein, C3, CFHR1/3/5, thrombomodulin, or autoantibody to factor H in DEAP HUS) causes complement-mediated endothelial damage. STEC HUS results from Shiga toxins (Stx1/Stx2, verotoxins) binding the glycolipid receptor Gb3 on renal microvascular cells, inducing inflammatory cytokines (IL-8, MCP-1, SDF-1) and chemokine receptors (CXCR4/CXCR7) with platelet aggregation; Streptococcus pneumoniae neuraminidase can expose the cryptic Thomsen-Friedenreich antigen so preformed IgM triggers MAHA. Scleroderma renal crisis features arcuate artery intimal/medial proliferation with onion-skinning, fibrinoid necrosis, and thrombosis. Antiphospholipid syndrome causes intralobular fibrous intimal hyperplasia and arterial/arteriolar occlusion. Renal vein thrombosis results from endothelial damage, venous stasis, or hypercoagulability (notably nephrotic syndrome, especially membranous nephropathy).

harrison.prognosis: Prognosis varies by subtype. Untreated immune-mediated TTP has a mortality exceeding 90%, and even with modern therapy about 20% die within the first month from microvascular thrombosis. HSCT-associated TMA is highly lethal, with roughly 75% mortality within 3 months. Scleroderma renal crisis historically had over 90% mortality at 1 month, reduced to about 30% at 3 years with renin-angiotensin system blockade; nearly two-thirds of patients may require dialysis, with renal recovery in about half (median ~1 year). HELLP syndrome carries a mortality of about 7.4-34% and usually resolves spontaneously after delivery. POEMS syndrome rarely progresses to end-stage renal disease. Renal injury in aHUS can be severe and progress to end-stage renal disease, with recurrence risk after transplant depending on the complement-regulatory protein involved. Chronic kidney disease develops in roughly 25-33% of sickle cell nephropathy patients, and nephrotic-range proteinuria predicts progression to renal failure.
pitfalls: Waiting for the full TTP pentad before acting is a mistake, since fewer than 5% of immune-mediated TTP cases display all five features.

Assuming TMA always shows MAHA can mislead: TMA is usually but not always accompanied by microangiopathic hemolysis, and in antiphospholipid syndrome renal TMA is common while signs of MAHA and platelet consumption are usually absent.

Scleroderma renal crisis is histologically indistinguishable from malignant hypertension and the two can coexist, so renal biopsy is recommended for atypical renal involvement, especially when hypertension is absent.
ADAMTS13 reduction in HELLP (30-60%) is milder than in TTP (below ~10%), so interpreting modest reductions as diagnostic of TTP can mislead during pregnancy when aHUS and TTP can also be triggered.

Thrombocytopenia in HIV-related TMA may prohibit renal biopsy, yet biopsy is required for diagnosis because other HIV-associated renal diseases mimic it; ADAMTS13 activity is not reduced in HIV-related TMA.
In drug-induced autoantibody TMA (e.g., quinine), disease can recur after even a single re-exposure in a previously sensitized patient, so it is not strictly dose-dependent.
Distinguishing HSCT-associated TMA is difficult because thrombocytopenia, anemia, and renal insufficiency are common after transplantation for other reasons.
harrison.severityClassification: No single unified severity scale; classification is by etiologic subtype and laboratory criteria. TTP is defined as MAHA with ADAMTS13 activity below 5-10% and subdivided into congenital (cTTP/Upshaw-Schulman) and immune (iTTP) forms. HUS variants include STEC/D+ HUS, pneumococcal neuraminidase-associated HUS, atypical complement-mediated HUS (aHUS), and DEAP HUS. HSCT-associated TMA has formal diagnostic criteria (Harrison Table 329-1): the International Working Group requires schistocytes (over 4% in one set, or RBC fragmentation with at least 2 schistocytes per high-power field), de novo/progressive thrombocytopenia, rising LDH, falling hemoglobin or increased transfusion need, negative Coombs, falling haptoglobin, and concurrent renal/neurologic dysfunction without other explanation. Antiphospholipid syndrome severity is stratified by antibody profile, with 'triple positivity' conferring the highest thrombosis risk and a catastrophic variant defined by rapid multiorgan failure.
management: Treat thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura urgently with plasma exchange plus corticosteroids, adding the anti-von Willebrand factor agent caplacizumab and rituximab for immune-mediated disease
Treat atypical complement-mediated haemolytic uraemic syndrome with terminal complement blockade using eculizumab, after meningococcal vaccination and antibiotic prophylaxis

Manage Shiga toxin-associated (STEC) haemolytic uraemic syndrome supportively with careful fluid and electrolyte balance and renal replacement therapy, avoiding antimotility agents and generally antibiotics
Provide renal support with dialysis for acute kidney injury, blood-pressure control and management of the microangiopathic haemolysis
Avoid platelet transfusion unless there is life-threatening haemorrhage, as it may aggravate microvascular thrombosis
Monitor serial platelet count, lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin, schistocytes, ADAMTS13 activity and complement studies to guide therapy and detect relapse
Refer to specialist nephrology and haematology and offer genetic counselling for complement-regulatory or ADAMTS13 mutations in congenital forms
